question_type: Absolute difference of two currencies' weekly FCP 'net options positions' converted to USD millions at each row's own exchange rate, for one mid-March 2016 weekly report date

opus_divergence.what_opus_did: Found the 03/16/2016 weekly rows in two printings, June 2016 and Sept 2016 (FCP-II-1 yen, FCP-IV-1 sterling). Correctly diagnosed that the June 2016 yen table is row-shifted: the row labelled 03/16/2016 is really the 10/21/2015 record. Opus realigned it. The net options values and the sterling row agree across both printings; only the yen exchange rate differs, and the Sept 2016 printing shows it with integer-looking precision. Opus judged the Sept figure to be display or precision loss, so it took the earlier June 2016 full-precision rate instead of the latest printing.
opus_divergence.what_right_glm_did: The prompt arm also saw that the June 2016 table was corrupted ([20]: dates and values misaligned). It did not realign that table. Instead it followed its adapter's self-check #1 ('compare it with the latest bulletin carrying the same row') and took every value, including the rounded-looking yen rate, from the latest printing (Sept 2016) ([22], [24], [26]). It computed with that rate at [34] and committed at [36].
opus_divergence.evidence: Opus: worklog.md:52-57 (Step 6 'exchange-rate vintage'); solution.json decisions[2] 'Issue vintage for the yen exchange rate'; review.md check 4 ('minor residual risk'). GLM prompt digest: [20], [22], [24], [26] (the full text in events.jsonl reads 'We should use latest bulletin carrying row (Sep 2016) because it's latest revision ... June table is corrupted'), [27] SAY, [34].

reviewer_flag: Verdict confirmed. The reviewer explicitly named the Sept 2016 (latest printing) yen rate as a 'minor residual risk' alternative, alongside the difference-of-magnitudes reading. It found no concrete error.
right_by_principled_choice_or_luck: Partly principled. The arm applied an explicit latest-printing rule from its adapter procedure, which at this point was only the base procedure with no lessons, and it correctly recognised that the June yen table was misaligned. However, it never realigned June, so it never saw June's full-precision rate for 03/16 and never faced Opus's choice between precision and recency. Its rule happened to match the key.
wrong_glm_arms_same_as_opus: No. The none arm ([33]-[39]) and the cards arm ([16]-[20]) both stayed in the June 2016 issue and took the row literally labelled 03/16/2016. That row is the misaligned 10/21/2015 record, the parse error Opus caught and rejected. Cards also skipped the billions-of-yen to millions conversion ([18]). Neither arm opened the Sept 2016 reprint. No GLM arm made Opus's choice (realign the June table and keep June's rate).
lesson_for_harness: The key follows the latest printing that carries the row, as it appears in the corpus text, even when that printing's values look rounded or degraded. Opus lost the point by overriding the latest-revision default on a 'precision loss' hypothesis and preferring an earlier, more precise printing. Suggested harness rule: when printings disagree and no issue is pinned, take the latest printing, and do not 'repair' it with an earlier printing's digits. The two wrong GLM arms show a complementary need: a check that compares the same dated row across adjacent issues would have exposed the June 2016 row shift.
notes: The two vintage choices differ by less than 0.2% in the final answer, so strict grading made this nuance decisive. Opus's diagnosis of the June 2016 misalignment (31 rows for 26 weeks, duplicated bottom rows) was correct. That misalignment is what defeated the none and cards arms (>25pct). The Sept 2016 tables print several other March rates, including one sterling rate, with obviously degraded precision, yet the key still used that printing. This suggests the question writer read the Sept 2016 issue directly. At this ordinal the prompt arm's AGENTS.md had only the base six-check procedure, and the cards deck was empty, so the adapters' learned content played no role.
